name: Dead Land
lines: The stone is too heavy to move tonight. Come back later.

"I went down a dark, tortuous stairway... through a dark passage, from which came a deathly, sickly odour, the odour of old earth newly turned." (Jonathan Harker's journal, Chapter IV.) The stair is the same here.

Fifty boxes of earth went from the chapel of Castle Dracula to Carfax, near London; the Count could rest only in the earth of his own land. These are a few of them, their lids loose, the earth inside damp and cold.
The niches hold the old dead of the Count's house: a crest worn away, a date that might be 14-something. Nobody comes to keep them now, in the Land of the Dead or anywhere else.
A branch of wild rose, laid on a coffin, keeps the Un-Dead inside it: so Van Helsing says in Chapter XVIII. Somebody has laid one here.

Dracula was written by Bram Stoker, an Irishman who managed the Lyceum Theatre in London, and published in 1897. It is told in letters, diaries, a ship's log and newspaper cuttings, all put in order by Mina Harker. The whole book is played from the great tomb: 27 chapters, from Bistritz to the castle in the snow.
A gold coin from the Count's heap

"A great heap of gold in one corner: gold of all kinds, Roman, and British, and Austrian, and Hungarian, and Greek and Turkish money, covered with a film of dust" (Chapter IV). One coin, very old, very heavy.
A handful of the Count's earth
Earth from one of the fifty boxes, carried from the chapel of Castle Dracula to Carfax (Chapter VII and XIX). Damp, cold, smelling of the grave.
"Doors, doors, doors everywhere, and all locked and bolted" (Chapter II). One of the keys to them, long and black with rust.
A wreath of garlic flowers
Van Helsing's garlic flowers, from Haarlem, rubbed round the window and the door to keep the Count out (Chapter X). Dried now, but they still smell.
A little gold crucifix
"For your mother's sake": the landlady's wife at Bistritz put her crucifix round Jonathan's neck (Chapter I). Somebody has hung one like it in the dark here.
A page from the Demeter's log
A page of the log of the Russian schooner Demeter, that came into Whitby harbour in the storm with a dead man lashed to her wheel (Chapter VII).
A broken Kukri blade
Jonathan's great Kukri knife, that swept at the Count's throat at the end (Chapter XXVII). Only a piece of the blade, notched.
You took it already: it is on your Relic Shelf.
Relics of the Count:
You have found them all.
❔ still somewhere in the vault
Seven relics of the Count lie about this vault. Look in the rooms.

⚰️ The tomb of Count Dracula. Cold air, and the smell of old earth. The stair down, the vault with its boxes, the niches; and at the far end, the great tomb with the one word on it. Press E there to walk the whole book. The way out is the iron door.
The Boxes of Earth
Something glints in the dust
The great tomb with the one word DRACULA
go down into the book

A little gold cross, hung on a niche
A rusty key on a nail

Dracula (Bram Stoker, 1897)
A torn page, water-stained
Something sharp in the dark
the Land of the Dead
Doña Refugio, a grandmother
a grandmother who died in 1961 in Oaxaca and comes back each year to her family's ofrenda; warm, a little bossy, proud of her mole
Mija, mijo, did they put out the mole? I can smell it from the river. Every year they forget the salt, and every year I forgive them.
Valentina, a soldadera
a soldadera, a woman who fought in the Mexican Revolution in 1913, with a rifle and a bandolier, brave and laughing
They sang songs about us, you know. 'La Adelita'. I never heard them; I was too busy marching. Now I hear them every year on this road.
Itzcóatl, an eagle warrior
an Aztec eagle warrior who died in battle five hundred years ago; those who die in battle walk with the sun, so he only visits
We who die in battle go east with the sun for four years, and come back as hummingbirds. I came back as a hummingbird. I am visiting as a man, for tonight.
Paquito, a little boy
a little boy who died of a fever in 1918; the little ones come first, on the first of November, the day of the angelitos
My mamá puts out toys for me, and sweet bread, and a little cup of chocolate. I come first, before the grown-ups. That's the rule!
Mr. Jonas Pell, a drowned sailor
an English sailor drowned off Veracruz in 1883, who found his way here and never left, polite and puzzled
Took a wrong turn at the river, I did. Very hospitable people. They put out a cup of rum for me every year, though I'm nobody's.
Don Chuy, a mariachi
a mariachi violinist who died in 1974 and still plays for the dead on their night
Every year somebody asks for 'La Llorona'. Every year I play it. Sad songs are the happiest ones here.
Rosalía, in her wedding dress
a young woman who died on her wedding day in 1890; gentle, not sad any more
He married again, and was happy, and now he is here too, with both of us. It is very complicated and we laugh about it.
Maestra Inés, a schoolteacher
a village schoolteacher who died in 1952 and taught three generations to read
Read to your children. That is all. Read to them, and one day they will put a book on your ofrenda.
Don Anselmo, a farmer
an old farmer of maize and beans who died in 1930; slow, kind, smelling of earth
The marigolds lead us home. The smell is strong, you see, and we have no eyes to speak of. A path of petals, and we follow.
Fray Bernardino, an old friar
a Spanish friar of the 1500s who wrote down the old Aztec teachings of the road to Mictlán in a great book, the Florentine Codex
I wrote it all down, what the old men told me: the river, the dog, the mountains, the wind of knives. Nine places, four years. Ask the xolo by the river if you would walk it.
Captain Emilio Carranza
a Mexican aviator who died in 1928 flying home from New York, still in his flying jacket
They built me a monument in the woods where I fell. Very kind. I prefer this: the lanterns, and the music, and nobody making speeches.
Lupita, a little girl
a little girl who died in 1999, who comes back with the angelitos and plays tag on the marigold path
You can't catch me! I'm a ghost! ... That's not fair, you're not even trying.
Día de Muertos, the Day of the Dead

This is the land where the dead come home, on the night when the living remember them: Día de Muertos, the 1st and 2nd of November. Families build ofrendas (altars) with photographs, candles, bread of the dead, sugar skulls and orange marigolds (cempasúchil), whose strong smell and bright colour are said to guide the spirits home.
The little ones, the angelitos, come on the 1st; the grown dead on the 2nd. Families keep vigil all night in the cemetery, at graves dressed in marigolds and candles, with music and food.

Before Spain came, the Mexica (Aztecs) told of Mictlán, the land of the dead, nine places deep: a journey of four years with a dog to guide the soul across the river. Find the xolo dog by the river to walk the road to Mictlán.
In the far corner of the panteón is an old foreign tomb nobody tends, with one word over its iron door. Go in: it is the way into the whole of Bram Stoker's Dracula.

Señora Ochoa, keeping vigil
a living woman keeping vigil all night at her family's grave, with candles and a thermos of hot chocolate
We stay all night. My grandmother is here somewhere, I can feel her. Sit with us a little, if you like. There's chocolate.
The tomb of Count Dracula
An old foreign tomb
The foreign corner
Nobody here remembers who is buried in the grey tomb in the corner, so nobody puts marigolds on it, and no candle burns. The word over its iron door is DRACULA.
Go in at the iron door, down into the vault. At the far end is the great tomb: press E there to walk the whole of Bram Stoker's Dracula (1897), 27 chapters.
The xolo by the river

A small hairless dog, grey-black, with a wise face, sits by the bridge as if he has been waiting for you. The old people said every soul needs a dog to guide it over the river of the dead: a xoloitzcuintli, the dog of the god Xólotl. Families kept them, and when someone died the dog went with them.
What did the old people say a soul needs to cross the river of the dead?
A dog to carry it over
The xolo wags his tail and trots off over the bridge. Follow him to the far bank.
Apanohuaya, the river
Apanohuaya, the first place

The river is wide and dark here. The Florentine Codex says the soul came first to a great river, and crossed it on the back of its dog: a yellow dog, they said, for a white dog would say "I have just washed myself" and a black one "I have just been dirtied". The xolo wades in; you hold on.
In the old telling, which dog would carry you across?
A white dog, because it is clean
A black dog, because it is strong
A yellow dog: the white and the black make excuses
Over, and wet to the knees. Up ahead, two mountains, very close together.
Tepeme Monamictlan, where the mountains meet
Where the mountains meet
Two mountains stand so close that the path runs between them, and the old telling says they crash together and part again. The dead must go through at the right moment.
How do you pass between the meeting mountains?
Climb over the top
Wait until they part, and go through quickly
A rumble behind you as they close. You are through.
Iztepetl, the hill of obsidian
The hill of obsidian
A hill of black glass, all edges. Obsidian is real: volcanic glass, sharper than steel, which the Mexica made into knives and mirrors. The dead must climb it.
Black volcanic glass
Carefully, step by step, over the top.
Itzehecayan, the wind of knives
The wind of knives
Up here it snows, and the wind cuts like obsidian blades. The old telling says the dead were burned with their clothes and goods so they would have something against this wind.
What did the families give the dead for the cold of the wind of knives?
Their clothes and goods, burned with them
Nothing: the dead feel no cold
You pull your coat round you. The xolo presses close, warm, and you go on.
Pancuecuetlacayan, where the dead float like flags
Where the dead float like flags
Tall banners stream in a wind that comes from nowhere. Here, the telling says, the souls are lifted and blown about like flags, and must hold on.
What do you hold on to, here?
The xolo, who is low and heavy
The wind drops. Ahead, something whistles past.
Temiminaloyan, the place of arrows
The place of arrows
Arrows stand in the ground everywhere, still quivering, shot by no one you can see. The dead walk on through them.
What should you do in the place of arrows?
Keep walking, and not be afraid
Pick up the arrows
Not one touches you. Ahead, eyes in the dark, green and gold.
Teocoyocualloyan, the jaguars
Stone jaguars, or real ones, it is hard to tell in the dusk. The old telling is fierce here; the land's telling is gentle: the jaguars look into your heart, and let the brave go by.
The jaguars sniff at you. What do you do?
Stand still and let them look
A rough tongue on your hand. They let you go by.
Izmictlan Apochcalolca, the narrow waters
A dark water in a narrow place, and a mist so thick you cannot see your own hands. The xolo knows the way by smell.
How do you find your way through the mist?
Wait for the mist to lift
His tail in your hand, step by step. The mist thins. Steps of stone, going up.
Mictlán, the house of the Lord and Lady of the Dead

The ninth place: a great stepped house of stone, and on its top Mictlantecuhtli, the Lord of the Dead, and Mictecacihuatl, the Lady, who keeps the bones of the dead and, they say, keeps the Day of the Dead itself. The journey has taken four years in the old telling. The Lady smiles at you: "You have come all the way. Now, go home for the night: they are waiting for you, with marigolds."
The souls brought gifts to the Lord and Lady of the Dead at the end. What were they?
The paper, cloth and gifts their families gave them at the burial
Flowers they picked on the road
You lay down your gift. The Lady gives you a marigold, bright as a lamp. Go home: back over the marigold bridge to the ofrendas in the plaza.
Home: the ofrendas in the plaza
Home for the night

The candles are lit, the bread is out, the marigolds smell of home. This is why the families build the ofrendas: so the dead can find their way back for one night a year, and be remembered. You put your marigold from Mictlán on the altar.
Why do the families put out marigolds (cempasúchil)?
Their colour and strong smell guide the dead home
🌼 The Road to Mictlán: walked. You keep the marigold from Mictlán. The spirits nod to you as you pass. Walk it again whenever you like.
You have been here.
Not yet. The road to Mictlán goes in order: next is
The Road to Mictlán ·
🐕 The xolo tilts his head. Not that: think again.
start the road to Mictlán
lay down the marigold
Fray Bernardino, by the river
Fray Bernardino de Sahagún, the Spanish friar who wrote down the old Mexica teachings of the road to Mictlán in the Florentine Codex in the 1570s; a gentle old scholar, now a spirit

The xolo by the bridge will take you, if you ask him. Nine places, the old men told me: the river, the meeting mountains, the obsidian hill, the wind of knives, the flags, the arrows, the jaguars, the narrow waters, and Mictlán. Go gently.
